"This is crazy!" my wife said. "New York has never gotten this much tourism, and it's fucking New York!"

"I know, it's like the entire city has been transformed into an American Mecca."

We were sitting at the table. It was morning, and she was taking quick sips of her coffee so as to not burn her tongue. I was happily scarfing down an omelette that I had cooked not five minutes ago.

She turned on the TV.

"New reports have come in about the portal to the fabled Garden of Eden that has opened up in New York. Our sources are telling us the line to look into the hole is over eight miles long," the woman on the television said.

"Wow, that's incredible, Nancy," the man sitting next to her told her.

"It sure is, Phil. Now, what do you think about all this? I mean, surely some people think it's just small hole in Time Square."

I was only half paying attention. I had gone over to the sink to clean my dish and wash my hands, and the TV had entered my periphery. I was no longer really listening. But the two news anchors went on.

"Well Nancy, I think that the faith of these people is truly inspirational. They've traveled a long, long way, just to see a glimpse of paradise through a hole only a few inches wide."

"It truly is a sight to behold, Phil," Nancy said.

I walked over to my wife and gave her a kiss, and then sat back down on the table. On the TV, Nancy put two fingers on her ear.

"Well folks, we have a new report coming in. It seems that a man-" she paused for a moment, looking down. "N-no, I can't say that on- okay, okay."

She was talking to whoever was on the other side of her earpiece, and looked up after a moment, staring into the camera.

"Well folks, it seems that a man has put his penis inside the portal."

My wife spit out her coffee.

"What?" Phil said.

"Yes Phil, his penis."

"Well, that sure is a story to tell the grandkids, isn't it?" Phil joked. "Not many people can say they stuck their wiener in paradise."

My wife turned off the TV.

"That's enough, Adam," she said.

"I know," I answered. "It's time."

We stepped outside into the garden and walked to the back side of the house. I had the hedge clippers in my hand. We stopped. On the back wall of the house, there it was. A large, flaccid dingaling sticking right out of our home.

"You ready, Eve?"

"I've got the duct tape right here."

"Okay, one, two, three."

I've worked heavy rotations, where highway patrol called us because of an 18 wheeler rolling over, to retrieving vehicles for the fire department to remove the body. AMA about my over 10 years of experience.
IAMA 11 year veteran of the towing industry. AMA!
Where's the most remote place you've ever had to tow from?
I live in a city, and rarely do I leave the area to pick one up. I've taken vehicles as far as PA on a truck though. Just recently I towed one 365 miles.
Have you ever had a vehicle owner lash out on you violently ?
Yes. One of the first illegal parking tows I did, the owner hit me with the car. Nothing damaging, just eye opening. I was hoping, and it was a pissing match of sorts. He won.
Has your tow truck stopped working while you were towing a vehicle?

Yes, more than once. When that happens you call two trucks. One for the vehicle you're towing, and a bigger one for you. It's a bigger problem when it shuts down completely because you don't have the ability to unload your vehicle. No power = no hydraulics. It's much nicer when it overheats because you can at least run the equipment in short bursts.
What was the most expensive vehicle you have towed? Where/what was the violation?

Either an Aston Martin DB7 or a Ferrari F355. The Ferrari had broken down and I towed it to Norfolk, VA. The Aston Martin was a guy I knew, who needed it to go to the dealer but didn't want to take the time to drive it there.

coincidence, I live in Norfolk, VA. Sadly, I don't own a Ferrari.

Thanks
What is the most messed up (external or disgusting interior) you had to tow?

This Ford Taurus full size wagon had to be the worst damage wise. This is why I'm an ass about drinking and driving. I've never done it, and get really pissed about those who do. Two people lost their lives the night I recovered this.
Wow sorry, I don't envy some things you have to see. I forgot for a while there it's not just picking up vehicles with a illegally parked or seized engine.

By far the worst thing I've been involved in was returning a vehicle to the scene of a fatal hit and run. A 15 year old boy was killed by a drink driver (seriously, fuck you if you drive after drinking) while taking pictures of his brother on a skateboard in their front yard. I brought the car back because they needed to match "parts". Small rural area and we helped mark off the scene. It involved measuring distances of items like shoes, glasses, etc. He laid in the yard, covered, while everything was processed. A family member sat with his body the whole time. Remembering it makes me sad.

Edit: You eventually become very good at compartmentalizing while working. I picked up a motorcycle accident and didn't realize until the next day I knew the guy, and had been at his house a week prior to his death.
Ever done any repo work and if so any violent exchanges.

I have done repo work, but the stuff you see on TV is for TV. A good rule of thumb is this: repos know they'll go, illegally parked are the dangerous ones because they aren't expecting it. If you're in repossession, you know they're looking for it. The guy parked at the hotel who's going to the restaurant down the street didn't expect to have his car taken, and is in a flash point of anger. They're dangerous.
Does your company deal mostly with requests from owners towing their own cars or business towing other people's cars?

We are strictly AAA. Any call we run comes through AAA. I've worked for a total of three companies over the years, and the first centered around auto shipping. Executive moving from Redmond, WA? Company would load their belongings into a moving truck, then their car into a car hauler (18 wheeler) and drive everything across the country. We would receive the car at our lot, then deliver it to their new home for them. Lots of executives, lots of expensive/cool cars. The second company was a contractor for AAA and we did AAA calls along with other commercial accounts. This company focused on money only. Illegal parking, impounds, rotations (police initiated tows), repossessions (very seldom). My current company does only AAA. We're the fleet. We only come when you ask, which is nice.

Being capable of using the gravity gun in Half Life 2 to kill a Combine elite with a flying toilet.

So many to choose from...

Well, the portal gun is a pretty obvious one. VVVVVV switching gravity rather than jumping made it really memorable. Fez's 2D -> 3D thing is also really cool. But I'd have to say my favorite mechanics can all be found in the game Antichamber. The puzzles involving perception, non-euclidean space, and general mind fuckery are all really cool. The block puzzle bits of Antichamber are kind of dull, though.

I just like to bend reality.

Perma-death. I love the challenge and the tension it creates when any step could be your last and force you to start from scratch. And I do love rogue-likes. This is probably a reaction to how easy games have gotten in the last decade and a bit though.

Rouge-likes and perma-death are two of my favorite things. Having a game properly incorporate the two and really give you a run for the money creates a sense of accomplishment when you finally get past a milestone. My win streak in Binding of Isaac is currently around -30 but I still love every game like it is my first.

I really like when my character becomes better at something by doing it. For example, GTA: San Andreas had you become a better driver, shooter, etc., just by doing that action. Skyrim does it pretty well, too.
Games with real time dynamic combat like chivalry. Chivalry has had many problems but the game slasher looks promising.

Hm... that's tough.

Minecraft's procedurally generated 3d world really blew my mind when I first picked it up years ago. I remember just walking in a straight line for more than an hour, taking it all in.

Fallout's VATS system is awesome too. Adds a pretty unique twist to combat.

I'm a sucker for little quirks in movement also. Rocket jumping, crouch jumping, etc. It can be immersion breaking, but awesomely fun if it fits into the game.
The Headshot. Such an addictive and rewarding game mechanic.
I like being able to script my AI companions' behaviors like in Dragon Age Origins and Final Fantasy XII.
Not my favorite but what of the fun and interesting for me: Skiing in Tribes: Ascend and surfing in Team Fortress 2

Microgames in RPGs, examples including Final Fantasy 6 and Southpark: Stick of Truth. I think that by giving each character it's own unique mechanic it not only adds to the gameplay, but also the identity of that character as a fighter. It makes them more memorable.

I know it has a bad reputation because of some games and companies using it to heavily monetize but I really love booster pack type things and lottery systems with cosmetic items. Sometimes its fair for everyone and not pure pay to win and when it is done right it is very addicting and adds a sort of prestige to some items.
FIFA gets me on this mechanic every year.

A bit cliche, but there is something immensely satisfying about a good old-fashioned double-jump (e.g. Metroid, Castlevania). Especially when you've earned it after hours of looking at ledges just out of reach with a normal jump.
Level up! I'm like "hell yeah, now I'm unbeatable!!" I usually die 3 seconds later doing some dumb shit.
Levolution! When done right at least. Being able to level a skyscraper changing the tactical possibilities of the battle or making a huge hole in the wall is really cool IMO.
having the freedom to make choices. perk trees are also gamer crack

I love 1 hit death like in hotline miami. Free movement combat like in dark souls is always fun (so many things are automatic in modern games, it's boring to me), perma-death, physical checkpoints at reasonable distances, etc.

I don't know if you can call that a mechanic in itself but 3rd person view. I think first person is really overused, I just feel like I'm handicapped because it's harder to see my surroundings, I'm just forced into that narrow point of view with my big gun in the bottom right corner and I can only see what's right in front of me. It can get kind of fixed by changing fov but it's still annoying and boring to me, the only valid argument I can see in favour of that is immersion but I've never been as immersed in a game as in a properly challenging 3rd person game like MGS, dark souls or hotline miami.

I like when games are challenging and these things make the challenge fun as opposed to the overpowered enemies you get when you set your game on hard mode in most games.

Free flowing combo based combat. And by that I don't mean the Arkham combat system. I mean the one used in the KH games or Okami. Where every input results into an action. It results in a combat that feels like you are in charge. Something I personally didn't get from the "free flow" in the arkham games. It sounds simple but it is absurd how few games actually have it.

Sidekicks/NPC helpers. Idk if I'm just lonely or something, but having a good companion (one that actually helps you fight and doesn't just stand around like a sack of precious flour) is really nice. Also don't give me the 'but they give you health/money sometimes bullshit,' they can pick up a gun/sword and fight too.
